q: The First Amendment Act of 1951, besides adding the Ninth Schedule, also:
options: added the words 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic' to the Preamble and expanded the Eighth Schedule to fourteen languages
created the office of the Deputy Prime Minister
abolished the Part IV of the Constitution
introduced the anti-defection law in the Tenth Schedule
explanation: The First Amendment Act of 1951 inserted the Ninth Schedule, enlarged the Eighth Schedule from eight to fourteen languages, added the words 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic' to the Preamble and set out the procedure for amending the Constitution in Article 368.

q: The 'Seventh Amendment Act, 1956' is notable for:
options: creating the office of the Vice-President of India
abolishing the Part A, B, C and D classification of the States and revising the First Schedule
introducing the Goods and Services Tax
abolishing the privy purses of the princely states
explanation: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 was given constitutional status by the Seventh Amendment, which abolished the four-fold classification of the States and recast the First Schedule in terms of the new linguistic States.

options: the abolition of the office of the Governor-General
the introduction of the collegium system
the division of the Seventh Schedule into three lists
the creation of the Eleventh Schedule
explanation: The Sixth Amendment divided the Seventh Schedule into the Union List, the State List and the Concurrent List, and the Third Amendment of 1952 had already added the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas.

options: the extension of voting rights to all adults
the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax
the creation of the Tenth Schedule
the addition of the Fifth and Sixth Schedules dealing with tribal areas
explanation: The Third Amendment of 1952 added the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for the administration of tribal areas, and the Fourteenth Amendment later replaced these two with the present Fourth Schedule.

options: the introduction of the National Judicial Appointments Commission
the abolition of the Council of Ministers
the creation of the Planning Commission
a separate elector for the election of the President and of the Vice-President
explanation: The Ninth Amendment provided for a separate electoral college for the President and the Vice-President and made provision for the election of the Deputy Speaker as Speaker when the vacancy is caused by death or otherwise.

options: the Eleventh Schedule containing twenty-nine subjects relating to Panchayats
the Twelfth Schedule relating to municipalities
the Tenth Schedule on defection
the Ninth Schedule of laws protected from judicial review
explanation: The Tenth Amendment added the Eleventh Schedule with twenty-nine items that may be devolved to Panchayats, and the Twelfth Schedule with similar items for municipalities was added by the Seventy-Fourth Amendment of 1992.

options: the introduction of the National Commission for Backward Classes
the extension of the Fifth Schedule provisions to the tribal areas of Assam
the creation of the Second Schedule
the abolition of Part VI of the Constitution
explanation: The Twelfth Amendment of 1962 extended the Fifth Schedule to the tribal areas of Assam, and the Fourteenth Amendment of 1963 then created the Fourth Schedule of seats for the Union Territories in the Lok Sabha.

options: the creation of the office of the Lokpal
the Second Schedule of emoluments
Part IX containing the Panchayats and the Eleventh Schedule
the abolition of the office of the Governor-General
explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment inserted Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule for Panchayats, and the Seventy-Third Amendment of 1992 later gave the three-tier Panchayati Raj system constitutional status.

options: the Eighth Schedule of languages
the Second Schedule of emoluments
the Fourth Schedule of seats for the Union Territories
the Third Schedule of forms of oaths and affirmations for the members of the executive, legislature and judiciary
explanation: The Sixteenth Amendment added the Third Schedule setting out the oaths and affirmations for the President, ministers, judges and legislators, and the Seventeenth and Twentieth Amendments also touched this Schedule.

options: abolished Part IV of the Constitution and made consequential changes
created the office of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
introduced the Tenth Schedule
abolished the Legislative Councils of the States
explanation: The Nineteenth Amendment of 1966 abolished Part IV, which contained the Directive Principles, on the argument that they were more appropriately placed in the Fundamental Rights chapter, and it also amended Part III and the Seventh Schedule.

options: the Seventh Schedule of distribution of powers
the Third Schedule of oaths
the Tenth Schedule containing the provisions about the disqualification of members on the ground of defection
the Eighth Schedule of languages
explanation: The Twenty-First Amendment of 1967 added the Tenth Schedule, which insulated the anti-defection provisions of the Tenth Schedule from the scrutiny of the courts, and the Fifty-Second Amendment of 1985 added the detailed provisions on the Tenth Schedule.

options: Article 21A and Article 45
Articles 39A, 44 and 48A
Article 32A
Article 300A
explanation: The Twenty-Third Amendment of 1969 added Article 39A on equal justice and free legal aid, Article 44 on a uniform civil code and Article 48A on the protection and improvement of the environment.

options: declared that no law amending the Constitution shall be subject to Part III and clarified the power of Parliament to amend the federal provisions
reduced the voting age to eighteen years
abolished the privy purses of the princely states
introduced the concept of a national emergency
explanation: The Twenty-Fourth Amendment of 1971 added the proviso to Article 13(4) and explained the proviso to Article 368(3) so that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is beyond challenge in a court on the ground that it abridges a fundamental right.

options: the creation of the National Judicial Data Grid
the abolition of the Council of Ministers
the abolition of privy purses and of the jurisdiction of the Privy Council in India
the introduction of the collegium system
explanation: The Twenty-Sixth Amendment of 1971 added Articles 395 and 396 abolishing the Privy Council's jurisdiction and the privy purses of the erstwhile princely rulers, and it also inserted the proviso to Article 361.

q: The 'Thirty-Eighth Amendment Act, 1975' and the 'Thirty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1975':
options: abolished the Lok Sabha
introduced the Tenth Schedule
reduced the term of Parliament
made sweeping changes to the emergency provisions so as to reduce the power of the courts
explanation: The Thirty-Eighth and Thirty-Ninth Amendments of 1975 altered Articles 352, 356, 359 and 360 and declared that the forty-fourth Amendment's safeguards were not binding on Parliament, and much of this was undone by the Forty-Fourth Amendment of 1978.

options: introduced the Goods and Services Tax
restored the safeguards for preventive detention, inserted Articles 39A, 43A, 44 and 48A and added the Panchayats to the Eleventh Schedule
created the National Commission for Women
abolished the office of the Speaker
explanation: The Forty-Third Amendment of 1977 restored Article 20 and Article 21 as safeguards against preventive detention, gave constitutional status to the Directive Principles inserted by the Forty-Second Amendment and added the Panchayati Raj items to the Eleventh Schedule.

options: restored the five-year term of the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies, renamed the Internal Emergency as the National Emergency and restored the courts' power to review an emergency proclamation
introduced the concept of cooperative federalism
abolished the Tenth Schedule
created the planning commission
explanation: The Forty-Fourth Amendment of 1978 undid much of the Thirty-Eighth and Thirty-Ninth Amendments, restored the five-year term of the House and the State Assemblies, required a special majority of Parliament to extend a national emergency and made the proclamation subject to judicial review.

options: introduced the Tenth Schedule
created the National Human Rights Commission
removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 300A
reduced the voting age to eighteen years
explanation: The Fifty-Eighth Amendment of 1988 deleted the right to property from Article 19 and Article 31 and inserted Article 300A, which provides that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law, with a proviso for compulsory acquisition for public purposes.

options: the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax
the creation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission
the extension of the freeze on delimitation
the insertion of Article 320A providing for a commission to consider the claims of the backward classes
explanation: The Sixty-Second Amendment of 1989 added Article 320A, which provided for the Mandal Commission and for a commission to investigate the conditions of the backward classes, and the Sixty-Fourth Amendment of 1990 gave the OBCs their constitutional status.

options: abolished the Part IV of the Constitution
inserted Article 320B creating a commission for the backward classes and Articles 330A, 332A and 334A providing for reserved seats
introduced the anti-defection law
reduced the term of the State Assemblies
explanation: The Sixty-Fourth Amendment of 1990 created the statutory commission for backward classes under Article 320B and inserted the provisions that allowed additional seats to be reserved for the backward classes in the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies.

options: Article 300A on the right to property
Article 21A on the right to education
Article 32A on national security
Article 164A providing for District Planning Committees
explanation: The Sixty-Ninth Amendment of 1992 inserted Article 164A requiring each State to establish District Planning Committees to consolidate the plans prepared by the Panchayats and the Municipalities.

q: The 'Seventy-Third and Seventy-Fourth Amendment Acts, 1992' also:
options: provided for the creation of the State Election Commissions and the District Planning Committees
created the National Judicial Appointments Commission
introduced the Goods and Services Tax
abolished the Legislative Councils
explanation: The two amendments of 1992 provided for the State Election Commission under Article 243K and 243ZA and for the District Planning Committee under Article 243ZD, apart from giving constitutional status to the three-tier Panchayati Raj and to the municipalities.

options: the creation of the Special Economic Zones
the representation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the municipalities
the voting age
the abolition of the Legislative Council of a State
explanation: The Eighty-Fifth Amendment of 2004 amended Articles 243D and 243-I and the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules to provide for reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Panchayats and municipalities.

options: abolished the office of the Deputy Speaker
introduced the Goods and Services Tax
inserted Article 21A on the right to education, substituted a new Article 45 and amended Articles 46, 47, 48 and 49A
created the National Commission for Backward Classes
explanation: The Eighty-Sixth Amendment of 2002 made the right to free and compulsory education a fundamental right under Article 21A and replaced Article 45 with a duty of the State to provide early childhood care and to secure elementary education.

options: limited the power of the States to impose taxes on the sale of petroleum products
created the National Judicial Appointments Commission
introduced the Goods and Services Tax
raised the period of reservation for the Anglo-Indian members
explanation: The Ninety-First Amendment of 2003 amended Articles 255(1), 256 and 263 so as to place restrictions on the States' power to levy taxes on the sale of petroleum products, in order to protect the interests of the Union.

options: the extension of the freeze on the population basis of delimitation
the delimitation of wards and the constitution of District Planning Committees for municipalities
the abolition of the Tenth Schedule
the creation of the National Commission for Women
explanation: The Eighty-Third Amendment of 2000 inserted provisions enabling the States to delimit wards and requiring the constitution of District Planning Committees in relation to municipalities.

options: introduced the Goods and Services Tax
created the National Judicial Appointments Commission
extended the freeze on the delimitation of seats
gave constitutional status to cooperative federalism through Article 280A and recognised the right to reside and earn in any part of India
explanation: The Hundredth Amendment of 2018 introduced Article 280A on cooperative federalism and added the proviso to Article 19(1)(g) guaranteeing the right of a citizen to move freely through the territory of India to reside and earn.

options: extended the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Tribes
introduced the Goods and Services Tax
constitutionalised the National Commission for Backward Classes
created the office of the Chief Election Commissioner as a three-member commission
explanation: The Hundred-Second Amendment of 2018 inserted Article 338B creating the National Commission for Backward Classes and amended Articles 342A and 342B, which was a long-standing demand of the Dalit leaders.

options: provided for reservation of up to ten per cent of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for the economically weaker sections
introduced the Goods and Services Tax
abolished the reservation for the Scheduled Castes
reduced the voting age
explanation: The Hundred-Third Amendment of 2019 inserted Article 330A and amended Articles 332A and 334A to provide for a maximum of ten per cent additional reservation for the economically weaker sections among the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

options: the abolition of the Legislative Councils of the States
the extension of the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and the ending of the nomination of Anglo-Indian members
the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax
the creation of the National Commission for Women
explanation: The Hundred-Fourth Amendment of 2019 extended the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes beyond 2020, ended the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha and allowed a member of the Anglo-Indian community to contest a general election seat.

options: the abolition of the Legislative Council of a State
the creation of a National Judicial Appointments Commission
the collegium system for the appointment of judges of the higher judiciary
the reservation of seats for women
explanation: The Hundred-Ninth Amendment of 2024 provides for a collegium comprising the Chief Justice of India and two senior-most judges of the Supreme Court for the appointment of judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts, and it also provides for a collegium for High Court Chief Justices.

options: the uniform civil code
the extension of the freeze on delimitation
the reservation of one-third of seats for women
the increase in the maximum strength of the Council of States from 238 to 250 members
explanation: The Hundred-Tenth Amendment of 2024 amended Article 80 to raise the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha from 238 to 250, with the additional members representing the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and the Anglo-Indian community.

options: reservation of one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies for women
the extension of the delimitation freeze
a uniform civil code
the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Tribes in the State Legislatures
explanation: The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam of 2023 provides for one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies, including the reserved seats, to be filled by women, with the provision to take effect after the next delimitation based on the first census after the amendment.

q: Under the Constitution, the power to amend:
options: is vested in the Supreme Court
is vested in the President
can be exercised by any State legislature on a subject in the State List
is vested in Parliament and is exercised in the manner prescribed by Article 368
explanation: Article 368 vests the constituent power in Parliament, and although the courts examine the validity of an amendment, the Supreme Court itself cannot add to or abridge the Constitution.

q: The 'basic structure doctrine' propounded in the Kesavananda Bharati case holds that:
options: the Directive Principles have a higher status than the Fundamental Rights
Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is wide but not unlimited and cannot alter the basic structure
the Fundamental Rights can be abridged by Parliament by a simple majority
only the President can amend the Constitution
explanation: The majority opinion in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Article 368 confers a wide power of amendment but that certain basic features, including supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, judicial review and free and fair elections, cannot be abrogated.

q: The 'Shankara Prasad' case (1951) is significant because it held that:
options: the courts may add to the Constitution
Parliament may amend the Fundamental Rights by a simple majority
Parliament's power to amend the Constitution is subject to the limitations of Part III
amendments made after 1950 are void
explanation: In Shankara Prasad the Supreme Court held that the power to amend the Constitution is wide but not unlimited and is subject to Part III, and the view was later qualified by Kesavananda Bharati and Minerva Mills.

q: The 'Sajjan Singh v. State of Punjab' case (1965) is significant because it held that:
options: the President alone may amend the Constitution
Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights
the courts may strike down any amendment
the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is wider than the power of the legislature to make ordinary law
explanation: The Court distinguished constituent legislation from ordinary legislation, holding that the wider constituent power could be exercised only in the manner prescribed by Article 368, and this principle was reaffirmed in Minerva Mills.

q: The 'Golak Nath v. State of Punjab' case (1967) is important because it:
options: held that Parliament cannot abridge the Fundamental Rights by ordinary legislation
declared the basic structure doctrine
declared the right to privacy a fundamental right
held that the Directive Principles are justiciable
explanation: Golak Nath held that the Fundamental Rights have a transcendental and immutable position, and this led Parliament to enact the Twenty-Fourth Amendment of 1971, which was partly undone by the Forty-Third Amendment of 1977.

q: The Constitution of India is divided into how many Schedules?
options: Fourteen
Twelve
Eight
Ten
explanation: The Constitution has twelve Schedules, beginning with the First on States and Union Territories and the Eighth on languages and ending with the Twelfth on the subjects for municipalities.

q: The 'doctrine of eclipse' applies to a:
options: rule made by a subordinate authority
law enacted by a State legislature exceeding its powers
pre-existing law inconsistent with a subsequent amendment of the Constitution
ordinance issued by the President
explanation: Under the doctrine of eclipse, a pre-existing law inconsistent with a later constitutional amendment is not void ab initio but is eclipsed to the extent of the inconsistency, and the position was restated by the Supreme Court in the Shankara Prasad case.

options: 26 January 1950
9 December 1946
26 November 1949
15 August 1947
explanation: The Constitution was enacted on 26 November 1949 but came into force on 26 January 1950, the date chosen as the date of the adoption of the Constitution at the time of the first session of the Constituent Assembly.

options: the President of India on 26 January 1950
the Prime Minister on 26 November 1949
the Chief Justice of India on 26 January 1950
the members of the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950
explanation: The members of the Constituent Assembly signed the Constitution on 24 January 1950 and it came into force two days later on 26 January 1950, and no person in India has ever been born a citizen of India.

q: The 'Preamble' to the Constitution was first amended to add the words 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic' by the:
options: Fifty-Second Amendment Act, 1985
First Amendment Act, 1951
Seventh Amendment Act, 1956
Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976
explanation: The First Amendment Act of 1951 added 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic', the Forty-Second Amendment added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity', and the Fifty-Second Amendment added the words 'integrity' and 'fraternity' to Article 19 and to the Constitution.

q: The Constitution of India is divided into:
options: twenty-five Parts
eighteen Parts
twenty Parts
twenty-two Parts
explanation: The Constitution is divided into twenty-five Parts and twelve Schedules, and the Part IVA on Directive Principles was inserted by the Forty-Third Amendment and the Part IXA on municipalities by the Seventy-Fourth Amendment.

q: Under Article 56 of the Constitution, the President of India holds office for:
options: seven years
five years
six years
four years
explanation: Article 56 fixes the term of the President at five years, and the President may hold office beyond that period if the election to the next office is not completed, though he then cannot hold the office of profit.

q: The 'Ninth Schedule' of the Constitution was inserted by the:
options: Seventh Amendment Act, 1956
Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971
First Amendment Act, 1951
Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976
explanation: The Ninth Schedule was inserted by the First Amendment Act of 1951 to protect certain laws from judicial review under Article 13, and the Kesavananda Bharati judgment established that the power to add laws to it is limited by the basic structure.

q: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha may be removed from his office only by:
options: a resolution of the House passed by an effective majority after fourteen days' notice
an order of the President
a two-thirds majority vote of the House
a resolution passed by a simple majority of the members present
explanation: Under the rules, the Speaker can be removed only by a resolution of the House passed by an effective majority and after fourteen days' notice, a procedure that protects the office from being destabilised by the ruling party.

q: The 'President of India' — The President is a:
options: a ceremonial head with no constitutional role
supreme head of the executive with the real power of government
an elective monarch with absolute powers
nominal head of the executive, with the real power vested in the Council of Ministers
explanation: Article 74 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, but the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister exercises the real power, and the President acts on the advice of the Council, save in a few specified cases.

q: The President can be impeached for:
options: appointing a Governor of a State
violation of the Constitution
owning a particular political ideology
refusing to sign a bill
explanation: Article 61 provides a single ground for impeachment, namely violation of the Constitution, and the procedure requires a two-thirds majority in each House and a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House.
